idiom_name: email.message.EmailMessage (ordered header mapping + payload); broker properties + body bytes
implementation_notes: The standard library already ships the pattern: email.message.EmailMessage is an ordered mapping of RFC 5322 headers plus a payload, where set_content() adds or replaces the body together with the matching Content-Type and as_bytes()/BytesParser turn the whole thing into one serialized package. Messaging libraries expose the same split under other names - a broker API takes the body as bytes with the headers/properties as a separate argument (AMQP properties and headers, Kafka record headers) and hands them back separately to the consumer. An explicit envelope (a dataclass with headers and body plus to_bytes/from_bytes) is justified when the wire format is custom or the header set must be validated.
code_sketch:
from email.message import EmailMessage
import json

msg = EmailMessage()
msg["X-Correlation-Id"] = corr            # header section
msg["X-Message-Type"] = "order.created"
msg.set_content(json.dumps(order))        # body + Content-Type
wire = msg.as_bytes()                     # one package
pitfalls: Setting a header twice appends rather than replaces for repeatable fields, and get() returns only the first value - consumers expecting a single value silently ignore the rest.
set_content() derives Content-Type from the Python type (str becomes text/plain), so a JSON payload needs subtype='json' explicitly or receivers see text/plain.
A parsed EmailMessage can be mutated in place and shares nested parts by reference; forwarding requires copy() (or a fresh message) to avoid changing the stored original.
